findings.source_passage: The Titans, they say, hummed snatches when chipping out the craters for volcanoes; and the grave-digger in the play sings, spade in hand.
findings.source_locator: Ahab's speech about coffin-singing, midway through the chapter
findings.why_it_matters: This is a rhetorically distinctive, allusion-laden passage central to the chapter's voice and to Ahab's philosophising about death and labor; its Shakespearean grave-digger reference carries interpretive weight that critics have noted.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Ahab's speech about the Titans and the grave-digger, even in compressed form, before the Carpenter's reply about the caulking mallet.

findings.source_passage: the caulking mallet is full of it. Hark to it… there's naught beneath. And yet, a coffin with a body in it rings pretty much the same
findings.source_locator: Carpenter's reply and Ahab's follow-up about the sounding-board
findings.why_it_matters: The sounding-board exchange is interpretively central — 'naught beneath' is thematically resonant with the novel's nihilism — and the Carpenter's line about the mallet being 'full of it' is a distinctive comic-philosophical exchange the draft entirely drops.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sounding-board dialogue, including 'there's naught beneath' and the coffin-knock-against-the-churchyard-gate passage.

findings.source_passage: Art thou a silk-worm? Dost thou spin thy own shroud out of thyself? Look at thy bosom! Despatch! and get these traps out of sight.
findings.source_locator: Ahab's sudden outburst cutting off the Carpenter, near end of dialogue
findings.why_it_matters: This is one of the most rhetorically distinctive and quotable lines in the chapter, capturing Ahab's characteristic eruptive surrealism; its absence flattens the chapter's voice significantly.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Ahab's silk-worm outburst verbatim or near-verbatim before he goes aft.

findings.source_passage: He's always under the Line—fiery hot, I tell ye!… This wooden mallet is the cork, and I'm the professor of musical glasses—tap, tap!
findings.source_locator: Carpenter's soliloquy after Ahab goes aft
findings.why_it_matters: The Carpenter's comic interior monologue, including the Equator-cuts-Ahab-in-the-middle image and the 'professor of musical glasses' line, is voice-establishing and provides essential tonal counterweight to Ahab's soliloquy; it is entirely missing from the draft.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Carpenter's aside — at minimum the Equator metaphor and the tap-tap conclusion — as it is structurally and tonally indispensable.

findings.source_passage: There's a sight! There's a sound! The greyheaded woodpecker tapping the hollow tree! Blind and dumb might well be envied now.
findings.source_locator: Opening of Ahab's soliloquy marked '(Ahab to himself)'
findings.why_it_matters: This opening of Ahab's interior soliloquy is rhetorically distinctive and precedes the immortality-preserver passage; dropping it means the draft jumps to the middle of the soliloquy, losing the build-up that makes the philosophical climax land.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the woodpecker image and 'How immaterial are all materials! What things real are there, but imponderable thoughts?' before the life-buoy-of-a-coffin passage.

findings.source_passage: Now, then, Pip, we'll talk this over; I do suck most wondrous philosophies from thee! Some unknown conduits from the unknown worlds must empty into thee!
findings.source_locator: Final lines of the chapter, Ahab's closing address
findings.why_it_matters: Ahab's closing address to Pip — 'Some unknown conduits from the unknown worlds must empty into thee' — is interpretively and tonally crucial, defining Pip's role as mystical vessel; the draft replaces this with an invented scene of Pip alone in the cabin that has no basis in the source.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the invented Pip-alone scene and restore Ahab's closing lines to Pip verbatim, including 'unknown conduits from the unknown worlds.'

findings.source_passage: Faith? What's that?… Why, faith, sir, it's only a sort of exclamation-like—that's all, sir.
findings.source_locator: Dialogue exchange after the churchyard-gate question
findings.why_it_matters: This brief exchange is characteristic of Melville's ironic wit — Ahab literalising the word 'faith' — and its absence removes a significant tonal register from the chapter.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the faith/exclamation exchange; it is short and fits even a compressed draft.

summary: The draft preserves only the jack-of-all-trades speech and the middle of Ahab's soliloquy while dropping the Carpenter's soliloquy entirely, the silk-worm outburst, the sounding-board exchange, the Titans/grave-digger passage, Ahab's closing address to Pip, and the faith-exclamation joke, replacing the chapter's ending with an invented scene — multiple high-severity failures requiring full regeneration.
